Hear, best of the twice-born, what happened in my former body. I remember my birth, Brahmana; listen to me with attention.
mahabharata:13:10.49	I was a shudra before, much devoted to austerity, and you then, best of the twice-born, were a sage of fierce austerity.
mahabharata:13:10.50	Pleased then, Brahmana, with a mind to favour me, you gave me instruction in the rite for the ancestors, sinless one, on the mat, the kusha grass, and the offerings to gods and ancestors, best of sages.
mahabharata:13:10.51	By this fault of action you were born a priest; I a king, lord of brahmanas; see the turning of time. By instruction given for my sake you got this fruit.
mahabharata:13:10.52	For this reason, Brahmana, I laugh at you, best of the twice-born; I do not despise you, Brahmana, I laugh; you are my teacher.
mahabharata:13:10.53	My anger arises from the reversal, and my mind is tormented by it. I remember my birth with you; therefore I laugh at you.
mahabharata:13:10.54	Thus your fierce austerity was destroyed by giving instruction. Leaving the priesthood, strive again in the next life.
mahabharata:13:10.55	Do not get from here another lower womb, twice-born; take wealth, Brahmana; become pure in soul, good one.
[Bhishma said:] Then, dismissed by the king, the brahmana gave many gifts to brahmanas, wealth, land and villages everywhere.
Having performed the penances as prescribed, that best of the twice-born went to sacred fords and gave various gifts.
Having given cows to brahmanas, the brahmana became pure in soul; going to that same hermitage, he practised great austerity.
Then that brahmana, best of kings, reached supreme success, and became honoured among the dwellers of that hermitage.
Thus that sage, best of kings, met great hardship; therefore a brahmana should not speak to people of lower classes.
A brahmana, O king, should always avoid giving instruction; the twice-born who gives instruction would meet hardship.
A king should always seek by speech from the best of the twice-born; nothing should be told here to people of lower class.
Brahmanas, kshatriyas and vaishyas are the three twice-born classes; telling among these, O king, a brahmana is not corrupted.
Therefore the good should not tell anything to anyone in front; the course of dharma is subtle, hard to know for the unpractised.
Therefore sages honour silence and initiation; for fear of ill-spoken words, O king, they do not speak anything.
The righteous, rich in qualities, devoted to truth and honesty, struck by ill-spoken speech, incur wrongdoing here.
Instruction should never be given by anyone to anyone, for from instruction a brahmana would incur that sin.
Therefore, having considered, one wise and desiring dharma should speak; instruction made with truth and untruth injures.
When asked here, one should speak after deciding on the reversal; and that instruction should be given by which one would gain dharma.
All this has been told to you: when instruction is given, great affliction comes; therefore one should never instruct anywhere."
[Bhishma said:] On this I shall tell you as it was seen and heard: Rukmini asked in the presence of Devaki's son.
Seeing Shri blazing, lotus-faced, seated on Narayana's lap, the mother of Makaradhvaja, with eyes wide and lovely in wonder, asked out of curiosity:
Which beings do you serve here, and which, standing, do you not serve? Tell me truly, beloved of beings, mistress of the three worlds, daughter of a great sage.
Thus addressed, Shri then, in the presence of the goddess and Garuda's banner, the moon-faced one, pleased, spoke sweetly and charmingly:

I dwell in truth, in the fortunate, the bold, the skilled man who engages in action; I do not dwell in a man averse to action, nor in an unbeliever, a mixer of classes, an ingrate, one of broken conduct, of cruel conduct, nor in a thief, nor in one who envies his elders.
mahabharata:13:11.7	Those who have little energy, strength and essence, who rejoice or are angry here and there, in such men, goddess, whose desires are asleep, I do not stay.
mahabharata:13:11.8	He who asks for nothing for himself, he whose inner self is stricken by his nature, in men devoted always to little contentment, I do not live, goddess.
mahabharata:13:11.9	I dwell among the righteous, the knowers of dharma, the great-souled, those who serve elders, the self-controlled, the knowers of truth, the great-souled.
mahabharata:13:11.11	A woman who acts without looking at her scattered goods, who always speaks against her husband, who delights in another's house, shameless, such a woman I avoid.
mahabharata:13:11.12	A woman impure, who licks, devoid of steadiness, fond of quarrel, overcome by sleep, always lying down, such a woman I avoid.
mahabharata:13:11.13	I dwell among women who are always true, pleasing to see, endowed with good fortune, rich in qualities, devoted to their husbands, of auspicious conduct and adorned.
mahabharata:13:11.14	I dwell in carriages, in maidens, in ornaments, in sacrifices, in rain-bearing clouds, in flowering lotus-ponds and in the autumn lanes of stars.
mahabharata:13:11.15	In mountains, cow-pens and forests, in lakes with blooming lotuses, in rivers sounding with the cry of swans and shining with the call of cranes,
mahabharata:13:11.16	in lakes adorned with wide banks, served by ascetics, Siddhas and brahmins, I dwell always in waters abundant, though waters troubled by lions and elephants; in a maddened elephant, a bull, a king, on a throne and in a good man always.
mahabharata:13:11.17	In whatever house a fire is offered to, cows and brahmanas are honoured, and the gods, and offerings are made in season with flowers, in that house I always take my dwelling.
mahabharata:13:11.18	I dwell in twice-born constant in study, in a kshatriya always devoted to dharma, in a vaishya devoted to farming, and in a shudra constantly engaged in service.
mahabharata:13:11.19	In Narayana I dwell with one mind, as his body, with my whole being; in him great dharma is established, and devotion to brahmanas and kindness.
mahabharata:13:11.20	I do not dwell by body, goddess; nor can I say it so here; in the man in whom I dwell by feeling, he grows with dharma, fame, wealth and desire.
[Bhishma said:] On this too they recite this ancient Itihasa, how the enmity of Bhangashvana and Shakra came about long ago.
Long ago there was a very righteous royal sage named Bhangashvana, childless, tiger among men, who performed a sacrifice for a son.
The royal sage, mighty, performed the Agnishtut, called hostile to Indra; it is prescribed among the expiatory rites for mortals who wish for a son.
Knowing that sacrifice, the greatly fortunate lord of gods, Indra, sought an opening against the self-controlled royal sage.
After some time, as the king roamed hunting, Indra, thinking "this is the opening," bewildered the king.
The royal sage, on a single horse, wandered, bewildered by Indra, and, afflicted by hunger and thirst, did not find the directions.
Running here and there, afflicted by fatigue and thirst, the king saw a very lovely lake full of excellent water; entering the lake, he watered his horse.
Then, having tied the horse that had drunk to a tree, the best of kings entered and bathed, and the king became a woman.
Seeing himself made a woman, the best of kings was ashamed, his whole self filled with thought, his senses and mind agitated.

How shall I mount the horse, how shall I go to the city? I performed the Agnishtut and have a hundred sons of my own body,
mahabharata:13:12.12	born, of great strength; what shall I tell them? And to my wives, and to the townspeople and countryfolk?
mahabharata:13:12.13	Softness, slenderness and timidity are said by sages who see the truth of dharma to be the qualities of woman; exertion, hardness and valour are the qualities of man.
mahabharata:13:12.14	My manhood is lost; how has womanhood come to me? In the woman's state, how can I again mount the horse?
With great distress he mounted the horse and the king came back to the city, dear one, become a woman, best of kings.
Sons, wives, servants, townspeople and countryfolk, wondering "What is this?", came to great astonishment.
Then the royal sage, become a woman, best of speakers, said: "I went out to hunt, surrounded by a strong army; bewildered by fate I entered a terrible forest.
In that terrible forest, thirsty, my senses lost, I saw a lovely lake surrounded by birds.
Plunging into it I became a woman, plainly by fate, without doubt, as if unsatisfied with sons, wives and wealth."
Then, become a woman, the best of kings said to the sons: "Enjoy the kingdom with affection; I shall go to the forest, my sons." Having consecrated the hundred sons, the king went to the forest.
In the hermitage an ascetic approached the woman, dear one, and by that ascetic a hundred sons were born to her in the hermitage.
Then she took those sons and said to the earlier sons: "You were my sons when I was a man; and these hundred are my sons as a woman.
Enjoy the kingdom together in brotherhood, my sons." Then the brothers together enjoyed the kingdom.
Seeing them enjoying the excellent kingdom in brotherhood, Indra, flooded with anger, thought: "A favour was done to this royal sage by me, not an injury."
Then, in the form of a brahmana, Indra Shatakratu went to the city and divided those sons of the king.

Brothers have no good brotherhood, even sons of one father: gods and asuras quarrelled over the kingdom, sons of Kashyapa.
mahabharata:13:12.27	You are Bhangashvana's sons, the others the ascetic's sons; gods and asuras too were sons of Kashyapa; your father's kingdom is enjoyed by the ascetic's sons.
Divided by Indra, they struck each other down in battle. Hearing that, the woman ascetic, tormented, wept.
Indra came in the guise of a brahmana and asked her: "By what sorrow tormented do you weep, fair-faced one?"
Seeing the brahmana, that woman said piteously: "Two hundred sons, Brahmana, have been destroyed by time.
I was a king, Brahmana, and a hundred sons were born to me there, handsome and valiant, best of the twice-born.
Once, going hunting, bewildered in a deep forest, I plunged into a lake and became a woman, best of brahmanas. Establishing my sons in the kingdom, I went to the forest.
And as a woman a hundred sons were born to me in a hermitage by the great-souled ascetic, Brahmana; I took them to the city.
Enmity has arisen between them by the union of time, twice-born; for this I grieve, lord of brahmanas, flooded by fate."
Seeing her in sorrow, Indra spoke harsh words: "Formerly, good woman, you made me suffer a hard sorrow.
You, sacrificing hostile to Indra, disregarded me, evil-minded one; I am Indra, ill-minded one, and I have repaid your enmity."
Seeing Indra, the royal sage fell at his feet with his head: "Be gracious, best of the gods; that sacrifice was for the wish of a son. Tiger of the gods, you ought to forgive me for that."
By the prostration Indra was pleased and gave a boon: "Which sons, king, shall live? Tell me, those born while you were a woman or those born as a man?"
The ascetic then, with joined palms, said to Shakra: "Those who were born to me as a woman, let them live, Vasava."
Indra, astonished and glad, asked her again: "Why are the sons you bore as a man hateful to you?
How is affection greater for those born when you were a woman? I wish to hear the reason; you ought to tell me."
[The woman said:] "A woman's affection is greater than a man's; therefore, Shakra, let those born to me as a woman live."
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed, Indra, pleased, said: "Let all your sons live here, truthful one.
And choose a boon, best of kings, whichever you wish, of good vows: manhood or womanhood, whichever you desire from me."
[The woman said:] "I choose womanhood, Shakra, since you are pleased, Vasava."
Thus addressed, Indra replied to her: "Why do you, having left manhood, prefer womanhood, lord?"
Thus asked, the best of kings, become a woman, replied: "A woman's pleasure in union with a man is always greater; for this reason, Shakra, I choose womanhood.
I delight more in womanhood, truly, best of gods; I am content with the woman's state; go, lord of the gods."
Saying "So be it," and taking leave of her, he went to heaven. Thus, great king, a woman's pleasure is said to be greater.
[Bhishma said:] God of gods and asuras' teacher, Vishnu, you ought to tell what Yudhishthira asks me, for Shiva of universal form.
The thousand names of the god were announced by Tandin, born of Brahma, in Brahma's world, as they were of old with Brahma.
Let Dvaipayana and the other ascetic sages of good vows and self-control hear what you say.
For the fixed, the delightful, the hotri, the protector, the creator of the universe, Agni, tell the greatness, lord, of the shaven, the matted-haired.
[Vasudeva said:] "The course of the deeds of the lord cannot be known in truth.
The gods headed by Hiranyagarbha with Indra and the great sages, who see the subtle, know neither his end nor his mind; how could he, goal of the good, be known by a mere man?
Of that slayer of asuras I shall tell some qualities of the blessed one, as they are, to you, for the lord of vows."
[Vaishampayana said:] Having so spoken, the blessed one, touching water and becoming pure, told the qualities of that wise great soul.

What I obtained very hard before for Samba's sake, and how I saw the blessed one before in concentration,
mahabharata:13:14.12	after Shambara had been slain by the wise son of Rukmini, when the twelfth year had passed, Jambavati said to me.
mahabharata:13:14.13	Seeing Pradyumna, Charudeshna and the other sons of Rukmini, desirous of a son, she came to me and spoke, Yudhishthira:
mahabharata:13:14.14	'Give me quickly, Achyuta, a son, a hero, best of the strong, of lovely form, spotless, equal to yourself.
mahabharata:13:14.15	There is nothing unattainable for you in the three worlds; you could create other worlds if you wished, lifter of the Yadava line.
mahabharata:13:14.16	By you, withering for twelve years as wind, having worshipped the lord of beasts, sons were born to Rukmini:
mahabharata:13:14.17	Charudeshna, Sucharu, Charuvesha, Yashodhara, Charushrava, Charuyashas, Pradyumna and Shambhu.
mahabharata:13:14.18	As sons of lovely valour were born to Rukmini, so give me too a mighty son.'
mahabharata:13:14.19	Thus urged by the goddess, I said to the slender-waisted: 'Give me leave, queen; I shall do your word.' She said to me, 'Go for victory and good.'
mahabharata:13:14.20	'Brahma, Shiva, Kashyapa, the rivers, the gods who follow the mind, the fields, the herbs, the sacrificial carriers, the metres, the troops of sages, the earth,
mahabharata:13:14.21	the oceans, the fee, the praises, the constellations, the ancestors, the planets, the wives of the gods, the daughters of the gods and the mothers of the gods,
mahabharata:13:14.22	the intervals of Manus, the cows, the moon, the sun, Hari, Savitri, the knowledge of Brahman, the seasons, the years, the nights,
mahabharata:13:14.23	the moments, the instants, the hours, the winks and the revolutions of the ages: may they protect you everywhere, Yadava, bringing happiness. Go your way unharmed, sinless one, and be vigilant.'
mahabharata:13:14.24	Thus having had the blessing said by her, I took leave of the daughter of the king of monkeys, and went to my father, the best of men, and to my mother and to King Ahuka.
mahabharata:13:14.25	Having told them the matter and what the daughter of the lord of Vidyadharas, greatly distressed, had said to me, I took leave then with great sorrow, and of Gada, Atibala and Rama.
mahabharata:13:14.26	Having got leave from my elders, I thought of Garuda; he carried me to the Himalaya and, having reached it, I dismissed him.
mahabharata:13:14.27	There on that best of mountains I saw wonderful things, and I saw a hermitage, best of fields of austerity,
mahabharata:13:14.28	the divine one of the great soul Upamanyu, Vyaghrapada's son, honoured by gods and gandharvas, joined with Brahmanic prosperity.
mahabharata:13:14.29	With dhava, kakubha, kadamba, coconut, kura, bakula, ketaka, jambu and patala, with banyan, varuna, vatsanabha and bilva, with sarala, kapittha, priyala, sala and palm,
mahabharata:13:14.30	with jujube, kunda and punnaga, ashoka, mango and atimuktaka, bhallataka, madhuka, champaka and jackfruit,
mahabharata:13:14.31	with many kinds of forest trees giving fruit and flower, crowded with flowering thickets and creepers, adorned with groves of plantain,
mahabharata:13:14.32	adorned with trees and fruits for the food of many birds, decorated with rows of forest placed in their places,
mahabharata:13:14.33	crowded with ruru deer, elephants, tigers, lions and leopards, full of antelopes and peacocks, with cats and snakes, frequented by herds of buffaloes and bears and other animals.
mahabharata:13:14.34	Mixed with the pollen of many flowers, scented with elephants' rut, rich in the songs of divine women, a pleasant wind blew there.
mahabharata:13:14.35	With the sound of streams, the cries of birds, the lovely trumpetings of elephants, the songs of kinnaras, and the noble sweet voices of Sama singers, hero.
mahabharata:13:14.36	Inconceivable even in mind to others, adorned with lakes, with great fire-shelters, covered with kusha grass,
mahabharata:13:14.37	adorned with the holy and pure water of the Ganga, king, ever frequented, adorned by great-souled sages, the best of upholders of dharma, like fires,
mahabharata:13:14.38	by wind-eaters, water-drinkers, constant mutterers, washers, ascetics constant in meditation, smoke-eaters, heat-drinkers and milk-drinkers, adorned on every side with the best of brahmanas.
mahabharata:13:14.39	Some who moved with cows, some pounders with stones, some with teeth as mortars, some drinkers of light rays, some foam-drinkers, some deer-roamers,
mahabharata:13:14.40	bearing very hard observances joined with great austerity, seeing them with eyes opened wide, I began to enter.
mahabharata:13:14.41	Well honoured by hosts of gods, by great souls, Shiva and the others, of holy deeds, that circle of hermitages shone always, king, like the sun's disc in the sky.
mahabharata:13:14.42	Mongooses play with snakes, tigers with deer like friends, by the power of blazing austerity, joined with the quality of nearness.
mahabharata:13:14.43	In that best of hermitages, pleasing to all beings, frequented by tigers of the twice-born who had crossed the Vedas and Vedangas,
mahabharata:13:14.44	by sages of many famous observances, great souls, as I entered I saw the lord wearing matted hair and bark,
mahabharata:13:14.45	blazing with splendour and austerity like fire, in the midst of pupils, calm, young, a bull of brahmanas. As I bowed my head, Upamanyu said to me:
mahabharata:13:14.46	'Welcome, lotus-eyed one; our austerities are fruitful, since you, worthy of honour, honour us, and you who should be seen wish to see us.'
mahabharata:13:14.47	With joined palms I asked about the welfare of the deer and birds, the fires, the dharma and the group of pupils.
mahabharata:13:14.48	Then the blessed one said to me in a very gentle conciliatory tone: 'You will gain a son equal to yourself, Krishna, without doubt.
mahabharata:13:14.49	Take up great austerity and please the lord Ishana. Here the god with his wife plays, Adhokshaja.
mahabharata:13:14.50	Here, long ago, gods with troops of sages, having pleased the best of gods by austerity, celibacy, truth and self-control, gained their lovely desires, Janardana.
mahabharata:13:14.51	The blessed one is a store of splendours and austerities; here, releasing and withdrawing things joined with good and bad, he stays with the goddess, inconceivable, whom you seek, slayer of foes.
mahabharata:13:14.52	The danava Hiranyakashipu, who shook Meru, got from Sharva the sovereignty of all the immortals for a hundred million years.
mahabharata:13:14.53	His chief son, famed as Mandara, by Mahadeva's boon fought Shakra for ten million years.
mahabharata:13:14.54	Vishnu's terrible discus and the thunderbolt of Akhandala were shattered on the limbs of that planet, dear one, Keshava.
mahabharata:13:14.55	The gods, harassed by the strong planet, in turn greatly slew the lords of asuras who had Shiva's boons.
mahabharata:13:14.56	Pleased, he gave even Vidyutprabha lordship over the three worlds; for a hundred thousand years he was lord of all worlds, and he said: You will always be my follower."
And the lord gave him ten thousand sons, and the unborn blessed one gave him the island Kusha as a kingdom.

Likewise a great asura named Shatamukha was created by the creator, by whom the fire was offered full a hundred years with his own flesh; the blessed Shankara, pleased, said to him, "What shall I do?"
Shatamukha said to him: "Let me have wonderful yoga, and give me, best of gods, eternal strength."
And Svayambhuva Kratu, too, long ago, for a son, entering himself by yoga, three hundred years,
to him the god gave a thousand sons equal to sacrifices. Krishna, you know the lord of yoga sung by the gods, without doubt.
The Valakhilyas, formerly disregarded by Maghavan, in anger pleased the blessed Rudra by austerity.
And to them the best of gods, lord of the world, pleased, said: "You will produce by austerity Suparna, the stealer of Soma."
Through Mahadeva's anger the waters were lost long ago, and the gods, with a seven-skulled vessel, sent others forth.
Atri's wife too, leaving her husband, a speaker of Brahman, saying "I will never again be under that sage's control," went to Mahadeva for refuge.
Fasting, from fear of Atri, she lay on pestles for three hundred years to propitiate Bhava.
Smiling, the god said to her: "You will have a son, and he will gain the fame you wish under your own family's name."
Shakalya, self-controlled, for nine hundred years worshipped Bhava by mental sacrifice, Keshava.
The blessed one, pleased, said to him: "You will be a maker of a text; your fame will be imperishable in the three worlds; may your family be imperishable, adorned with great sages."
And Savarni was a famous sage in the Krita age; he practised austerity here for six thousand years.
The blessed Rudra, directly pleased, said to him: "I am pleased with you, sinless one; you will be a world-famous maker of a text, ageless and deathless."
And how I myself saw the god of gods, the all-pervading, long ago, directly the lord of beasts, dear one, hear that too, Madhava.
And for what purpose Mahadeva of great splendour was worshipped by me, restrained, long ago, hear that too in detail.
All that I got before from the god of gods Maheshvara I shall tell you today in full, sinless one.
Long ago in the Krita age, dear one, there was a greatly famed sage named Vyaghrapada, who had crossed the Vedas and Vedangas; I was his son and Dhaumya my younger brother.
Once, Madhava, I came with Dhaumya to a hermitage, playing, of sages of purified selves.
There I saw a milch cow being milked, and I tasted the milk, sweet, like nectar.
Then, Madhava, flour was stirred in water and brought for us to drink as "milk".
Then once I drank cow's milk, dear one; the taste of the flour-water did not give me joy.
Then, from childishness, I said to my mother: "Give me food with milk and rice."
Then my mother, full of sorrow and grief, embraced me out of love for her son and, smelling my head, Madhava, said:

Whence milk and rice, child, for sages of purified selves who always live in the forest, eating roots and fruits?
mahabharata:13:14.83	Without propitiating the three-eyed, boon-giving, imperishable Sthanu, whence milk and rice, child, and comforts and clothes?
mahabharata:13:14.84	Resorting to Shankara always with your whole being, child, by his grace you will gain fruit of your desires, my son.
Hearing my mother's word, slayer of foes, from then on my devotion to Mahadeva became firm.
Then I took up austerity and pleased Shankara, standing on the tip of my toe for a divine thousand years.
For one hundred years I lived on fruit, for the second on fallen leaves, the third on water, and for seven hundred I lived on air.
Then Mahadeva, pleased, lord of all worlds, taking Shakra's form, surrounded by all the hosts of gods, becoming thousand-eyed, thunderbolt in hand, of great fame,
came on a great elephant, white as nectar, red-eyed, stiff-eared, in rut, with trunk curled, fierce, four-tusked,
the blessed one mounted it, blazing with his own splendour, crowned, adorned with necklace and armlets,
a white parasol held over his head, served by apsarases, resounding with divine gandharvas.
Then the lord of gods said to me: "I am pleased with you, best of the twice-born; choose a boon from me, whatever is in your mind."
Hearing Shakra's word, I was not pleased in mind, and I said these words to the king of gods, Krishna:

I do not want a boon from you, nor from any other god, except Mahadeva, gentle one; I tell you this truth.
mahabharata:13:14.95	At the word of the lord of beasts I would become a worm, or a tree with many branches; the glory of kingship over the three worlds, born of the favour of one not the lord of beasts, is also unwelcome to me.
mahabharata:13:14.96	Let me be an insect or a moth by Shankara's command; but, Shakra, I do not want even the three worlds given by you.
mahabharata:13:14.97	As long as my lord the blessed lord of beasts, with the spotless sliver of the moon bound in his crest, is not pleased with me, so long I bear the sorrows made in the body by hundreds of blows of old age, death and birth.
mahabharata:13:14.98	Radiant like sun, moon and fire, the essence of the three worlds, boundless, primal, one, ageless, deathless: without propitiating Rudra, what man in this world would find peace?
[Shakra said:] "What then is your reason regarding the lord, the cause of causes, that you do not wish favour from any other god?"
[Upamanyu said:] "What are other reasons to you? He is the lord, the cause of causes; we have not heard that the mark of any other is worshipped by the gods.
Whose lingam, other than Maheshvara's, is worshipped by all the gods, or was worshipped before? Tell, if you have heard.
Whose lingam Brahma and Vishnu and you with the gods always worship, therefore that is the best; he is the darkest.
Therefore I wish that boon, or even death, Kaushika; go or stay, Shakra, as you please, slayer of Bala.
Let this boon be mine, or a curse, from Maheshvara; and I wish no other deity, though they give the fruit of all desires."
Having so spoken to the king of gods, my senses agitated with sorrow, "Rudra is not pleased with me; what is this?" I thought; and in a moment I saw that same Airavata again,
like a swan, kunda flower and moon, shining like lotus fibre and water-lily, in the form of a bull, directly like the Milk Ocean.
Black-tailed, huge-bodied, with honey-yellow eyes, adorned on every side with a garland of gold,
red-eyed, with a great nose, fine ears, fine hips, fine flanks, broad shoulders, of fine form and lovely to see.
His hump shone, filling up the shoulder, like a snow-mountain peak, like the crest of a white cloud.
Mounted on it the blessed god of gods Mahadeva with Uma shone like the moon on the full-moon night.
From his splendour arose fire, with cloud and thunder, standing covering all like a thousand suns.
The lord of great splendour, like the fire at the end of the age, as if eager to burn all beings at the end of the age.
With that splendour spreading all around, hard to look at, again with agitated heart I thought: "What is this?"
[Brihaspati said:] "Having sacrificed for an immortal I will not sacrifice for a man; go or do not go, Marutta, I have turned back today from sacrificing."
But Gandhari, knower of dharma, bearing it greatly in mind, held back her sorrows, king, and said, "Do not be so."
Then, O king, the blessed Narayana of fierce splendour, the source and the imperishable, teacher of yoga, filling heaven and earth with his glory, reached his own immeasurable abode, the great soul.
Then, taking a divine body, Yudhishthira, the king of dharma, free of enmity and free of torment, plunged into those waters.
